outcome: A July 2026 preprint (Cheng & Sgueglia) proves an asymptotic version of Kotzig's perfect 1-factorization conjecture: K_n can be decomposed into n-1 perfect matchings such that (1-o(1))n of them pairwise form Hamilton cycles; the conjecture that ALL n-1 matchings can be made to pairwise form Hamilton cycles remains open.

ai.basis_quote: The construction in Theorem 1.3 is a generalisation of the one presented at the beginning of the Introduction and was generated by ChatGPT 5.4, which also gave a correct but rather long proof. The one presented here is a cleaner, shorter and substantially different one, and was obtained by the authors. The proof of Theorem 1.2 was entirely obtained by the authors.

summary: The conjecture (Kotzig, 1964): every K_2n, n>=2, has a perfect 1-factorization (a 1-factorization in which every pair of perfect matchings forms a Hamilton cycle). It remains open in general as of this writing. The one substantive development in the window is arXiv:2607.09459 'The perfect 1-factorisation conjecture holds asymptotically' (Cheng & Sgueglia, submitted 2026-07-10), which proves that for large even n, K_n has a 1-factorization in which a (1-o(1)) fraction of the n-1 matchings pairwise form Hamilton cycles (Theorem 1.2), building on an auxiliary near-optimal construction of edge-disjoint 'perfect pairs' matchings (Theorem 1.3) that cannot itself be extended to a full factorization. This is progress on the density/bound of the conjecture, not a resolution of any case n=2n0, and not a resolution of the conjecture itself -- it is squarely a 'bound moved on a problem that is still open' situation, so status is 'progress' with resolution_direction null per Section 6.4. On AI: the paper contains an explicit 'Comment on the use of AI' section (unusual and directly on point for this project) stating that ChatGPT 5.4 generated a correct construction and proof for the (superseded, more general) version of Theorem 1.3 presented at the start of the Introduction, but that the proof actually used in the paper -- for both Theorem 1.3 as stated and for the main result Theorem 1.2 -- was obtained entirely by the human authors, described as 'cleaner, shorter and substantially different.' Per Section 6.2, ai_role is coded on what mathematics from an AI system appears in the final result: since the authors state the AI-generated construction and proof were replaced by their own independent, different proof, and that Theorem 1.2 (the paper's main claim, on which this record's status rests) was 'entirely obtained by the authors,' no AI-produced mathematics survives into the published result, so ai_role is 'none.' The second triage-flagged paper (arXiv:2510.01949, Glock & Sgueglia, 'On Kotzig's conjecture in random graphs,' Oct 2025) addresses a related-but-different question -- existence of k edge-disjoint perfect-pair matchings in the random graph G(n,p) rather than a full 1-factorization of the complete graph K_2n -- and shows no AI involvement; it is a related problem under Section 3.1's scope test (changes the host graph from K_2n to G(n,p)), not a case of the stated conjecture, so it does not itself drive this record's status, though it corroborates recent research interest and shares an author and toolkit with the asymptotic paper. No resolution, no case settled exactly, and no counterexample were found anywhere in the window.
competing_reading: One could argue ai_role should not simply be 'none' but should be flagged as a near-miss 'incident'-adjacent situation: an AI system did produce a complete, correct, verified construction and proof for a real theorem in the paper's lineage (the more general version of Theorem 1.3), and its existence plausibly shaped the authors' confidence that the approach would work, even though the specific proof appearing in print was independently re-derived by humans. The rules in Section 6.2 are explicit that only mathematics 'in the final result' counts, and the authors are explicit that the printed proof is 'substantially different,' so 'none' is the correct code, but a reader focused on process rather than the artifact might weight this differently. Also debatable: whether the asymptotic result should be read as 'partial' (a case: 'for sufficiently large n, almost all pairs') rather than 'progress' (a bound). I read it as a bound because no specific n or Hamilton-cycle-pair count is exactly settled -- the o(1) term is never removed for any concrete n -- consistent with Section 3.1's guidance that a bound moving is 'progress' rather than a case being 'settled.'
what_would_settle_it: A full resolution would require either a proof that ALL n-1 matchings (not just (1-o(1))n) can be made pairwise Hamilton for all large even n, or a counterexample exhibiting some even n with no perfect 1-factorization of K_n at all. Absent that, expert digestion (e.g., a Tao-style blog treatment, or journal acceptance) of arXiv:2607.09459 would move it from a fresh preprint toward more firmly established progress, though the status code ('progress' on an open problem) would not change since the underlying conjecture is still unresolved either way.

judgement.doubts: Status progress is right: an asymptotic (1-o(1)) fraction is a bound, no n settled. The AI call hinges on reading the disclosure: 'The one presented here' most naturally refers to the proof, so the Theorem 1.3 construction printed in the paper is ChatGPT's, while its proof and all of Theorem 1.2 are human. If the authors meant the construction was also replaced, ai_role would be none. Theorem 1.3 is a result on the same bullet in the same event, so it counts under 'part of the mathematics in the result'.
